question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression
question.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 4x{e}^{8x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{8x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot {e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot \frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}-\int \frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x{e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{8x}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{8x}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{8x}}{16}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x+7\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{2x+5}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (x+7)\cdot {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =(x+7)\cdot \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\int \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+7){e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{(x+7){e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+7){e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
question.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 10x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=10x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=10 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 10x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =10x\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\cdot 10\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 10x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =10x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-10\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =10x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+10\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression
question.worked_solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x{csc}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={csc}^{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cot}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ where $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{csc}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⇒ & v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}-{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})]+\frac{1}{4}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4}]+\frac{1}{4}[0-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[0]+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
